problemText: A piece of land has water touching all of its edges on every side. It is not connected to any other land. What is this landform called?
choices: Isthmus
Peninsula
Island
Coast
hints: Trace the entire edge of this land with your finger. What do you find along every part of that edge?
The definition says this landform has no connection to any larger landmass at all.

problemText: A narrow strip of land has ocean water running along both its north and south edges for its entire length. At its western end, the strip widens into a large continent. At its eastern end, the strip widens into a completely different, separate continent. Is this strip an isthmus or a peninsula?
choices: A peninsula, because it is a narrow strip of land with water on at least one side throughout its length
A peninsula, because it widens into a continent only at one of its two ends
An isthmus, because the water surrounds it on both of its long sides and land appears at both ends
An isthmus, because it has water on both long sides and land at both ends
hints: Use the one-question check: does the narrow strip lead to more land at its far end, or does it leave you surrounded by water?
An isthmus connects two land areas, while a peninsula dead-ends in water. What happens at each end of this strip?

problemText: A mapmaker describes a piece of land in her invented region. Water touches its northern, eastern, and southern edges. Its western edge is attached to a much larger area of land with no water breaking the connection. Which landform is being described?
choices: A peninsula
An isthmus
An island
A coast
hints: Count how many sides have water and how many sides have land connection. Does water touch most sides or all sides?
This landform reaches out into water but stays attached on one side to a larger landmass.

problemText: Two narrow strips of land are described below. Strip A has water on both its long sides but leads to more land at both ends. Strip B has water on both its long sides but leads to more land at one end and runs out into open ocean at the other end. Which strip is an isthmus, and why does the other strip fail to be one?
choices: Strip B is an isthmus because it has water on both long sides and connects to at least one larger landmass; Strip A is a peninsula because one end does not connect to any land
Strip A is an isthmus because both ends lead to land; Strip B is a peninsula because one end reaches water instead of land
Strip B is an isthmus because it has water on two sides and touches two continents; Strip A fails because it is too narrow to be counted as land
Strip A is a peninsula because it is narrower; Strip B is an island because it is surrounded by water on both long sides and at one end
hints: An isthmus connects two land areas, not just one. Check the far end of each strip carefully.
A peninsula dead-ends in water on all sides except one. Which strip matches that definition better?

problemText: A student says, 'An island has no coast, because a coast is only found on mainlands.' Use the lesson definition of coast to explain why this statement is wrong.
choices: The student is correct because islands are surrounded by water, so they cannot have a coast along the edges where water meets land
The student is wrong because coast names wherever land meets an ocean or sea, and a peninsula has a coast, so the same must be true for islands
Coast names wherever land meets an ocean or a sea, so an island has a coast running all the way around it because water touches every side
The student is partially correct because coasts are found on mainlands and peninsulas, but islands have edges called shorelines instead of coasts
hints: Coast answers a different question than island, peninsula, and isthmus. It names a place, not a shape.
Think about what the word coast means: the edge where land meets an ocean or sea. Does an island have such an edge?

problemText: A geography student is shown three different landforms in her region and must sort them correctly. Landform X is a narrow strip with water on both long sides and land at both ends. Landform Y is reached only by crossing water no matter which direction you come from. Landform Z touches the ocean but is attached to a larger landmass on one side and surrounded by water on three sides. The student also needs to name the edge running along the ocean for each landform. Which pairing is completely correct?
choices: X is a peninsula, Y is an island, Z is an isthmus; all three have coasts along their ocean edges
X is a peninsula, Y is an island, Z is an isthmus; only Y has a coast all the way around
X is an isthmus, Y is an island, Z is an isthmus; only X and Y have coasts
X is an isthmus, Y is an island, Z is a peninsula; all three have coasts along their ocean edges
hints: Assign X, Y, and Z to their landforms using the one-question check: what is at the far end, and how many sides are attached to land?
Remember that coast is not the same list as the three shapes. Every landform that touches an ocean or sea has a coast somewhere along that edge.

problemText: Which water feature is defined by water that flows through a channel across the land, moving from higher ground toward lower ground?
choices: Strait
Lake
Sea
River
hints: Think about which water feature is always moving, not still.
This feature flows downhill in a channel, the way water naturally runs.

problemText: A body of water is completely surrounded by land on every side, with no place along its edge that opens to an ocean or a sea. The water is fresh, not salty. What is this water feature?
choices: Lake
Gulf
Strait
Sea
hints: Look for the clue about complete enclosure by land—which feature is fully enclosed with no opening at all?
This feature has land on every side, unlike a gulf or sea which always have at least one opening to larger water.

problemText: A ship enters a narrow stretch of water from a large open ocean. It sails straight through the narrow water, passing land on both its left and right sides, and exits into a different large body of water on the opposite end. Which water feature did the ship travel through?
choices: Gulf
Strait
Lake
Sea
hints: Notice that the ship enters from one body of water and comes out into a different body of water—this is a through-passage, not a pocket.
This feature connects two larger bodies of water end to end, not side to side.

problemText: Two water features are being described. Water Feature X is salty, has land curving around most of its edge, and connects back to the ocean through one narrower opening. Water Feature Y is fresh, has land all the way around it, and has no opening to the ocean anywhere. Explain why Feature X cannot be a lake and Feature Y cannot be a gulf.
choices: Feature X is narrower than a gulf should be, and Feature Y is too large to be a lake.
Feature X is too salty and Feature Y is not salty enough to be either water feature.
Feature X is salty but lakes are always fresh, and Feature Y has no opening but gulfs always keep one opening to the ocean.
Feature X connects to the ocean but lakes connect to rivers, and Feature Y connects to rivers but gulfs connect to oceans.
hints: Remember that lakes are defined by being completely enclosed with no opening, while gulfs are defined by having exactly one opening to the ocean or sea.
Salt water vs. fresh water, and the presence or absence of an opening to the ocean, are key properties that separate these features.

problemText: A geography student describes a water feature as follows: 'This body of salt water is bordered by land on part of its edge, and the rest of its edge stays broadly open to a larger ocean it connects with. You enter it and exit it through the very same opening.' Is the student's description complete and accurate for identifying this as a sea? Explain why or why not.
choices: Yes, the description is complete because it mentions salt water, land bordering part of the edge, and a broad opening to the ocean.

No, the description is incomplete because it does not distinguish between a sea and a gulf, since both are entered and exited through one opening but a gulf has a much narrower connection to the ocean.
No, the description is wrong because a sea must be surrounded by land on all sides except for multiple openings, whereas this feature only has one opening to the ocean.
No, the description is inaccurate because a sea is entered and exited through the same opening, but so is a gulf, and the student did not explain what separates them.
hints: Both a sea and a gulf are entered and exited through the same opening—so just mentioning that does not tell them apart.
What separates a sea from a gulf? Think about how broad or narrow the opening is, and how much of the edge is curved around by land.

problemText: A geographer is studying three water features in the same region. The first flows downhill through a channel, emptying into the second water feature. The second is completely enclosed by land with no opening to the ocean. The third is nearby and is salt water bordered by land on most of its edge, with only a narrow connection to the ocean. The geographer wants to name each feature correctly. Identify which feature is the river, which is the lake, and which is the gulf, and explain one property that makes each one impossible to confuse with the other two.
choices: The first is a river because it flows downhill; the second is a lake because it is enclosed with no ocean opening; the third is a gulf because salt water with mostly enclosed edges connects narrowly to the ocean. Rivers move through channels, lakes have no opening at all, and gulfs always keep exactly one opening.

The first is a river because it is smaller than the second feature; the second is a lake because it receives water from the first feature; the third is a gulf because it contains salt water instead of fresh water. The combination of size, position in the water cycle, and salt content determines the correct identification.

The first is a river because it flows into the second feature; the second is a lake because the first feature empties into it; the third is a gulf because it is bordered mostly by land but connected to the ocean. Each feature's relationship to the others and the presence of land and ocean connections define them.

The first is a river because fresh water flows through it; the second is a lake because fresh water collects in it; the third is a gulf because salt water fills it with land boundaries around it. The salinity of the water determines whether each feature is a river, lake, or gulf.
hints: Focus on the defining relationship between water and land for each feature, not on size, location, or just whether the water moves.
A river's defining feature is movement through a channel downhill; a lake's is complete enclosure with no opening; a gulf's is salt water with exactly one narrower opening to the ocean.

problemText: What does the word elevation mean in geography? Choose the best definition.
choices: How high a point of land sits above sea level
How much the height of the land changes across an area
How steep the hills are near a town
How far a place is from the nearest ocean
hints: Think about the word 'level' — elevation is measured up from a standard starting point.
Sea level is the shared reference line used for all elevations on Earth.

problemText: A place is described as sitting 150 meters above sea level, with the ground staying nearly the same height for miles around it. What is the elevation and relief of this place?
choices: High elevation and high relief
Low elevation and low relief
Low elevation and high relief
High elevation and low relief
hints: 150 meters is a small distance above sea level compared to mountains — is that high or low?
If the ground stays nearly the same height for miles around, is that much change or little change?

problemText: Two places both sit about 2,000 meters above sea level. Place A has ground that stays almost level for a long stretch. Place B has ground that rises and falls sharply within a short distance. Which statement is true?
choices: Both places have the same elevation and the same relief
The places have different elevations but the same relief
Both places have the same elevation but different relief
The places have different elevations and different relief
hints: If both places sit at about 2,000 meters above sea level, what does that tell you about their elevations?
The descriptions of the ground around each place are different — so check relief by itself, separate from elevation.

problemText: A student says: 'Highcliff sits 3,000 meters above sea level, so it must have high relief with steep cliffs and sharp drops all around it.' Highcliff is actually described this way: it sits 3,000 meters above sea level, but the ground around it stays nearly flat and level for a long stretch in every direction. What is wrong with the student's reasoning, and what is the correct description of Highcliff?
choices: The student mixed up the definitions of elevation and relief. Highcliff has low elevation and low relief.
The student wrongly assumed that high elevation means high relief. Highcliff has low elevation and high relief.
The student was correct that high elevation always means high relief. Highcliff must have high relief.
The student wrongly assumed that high elevation means high relief. Highcliff has high elevation and low relief.
hints: Look at what the student did — they looked at the elevation (3,000 meters) and then guessed about the relief without reading what the ground is actually like.
The description says the ground stays nearly flat and level — what does that tell you about relief, no matter how high the place sits?

problemText: Deepvalley sits about 80 meters above sea level. The ground right around Deepvalley rises steeply on all sides, with deep dips and sharp climbs. Plainridge sits about 1,800 meters above sea level. The ground around Plainridge changes very little, staying nearly the same height for miles. Which place has the higher elevation, and which place has the higher relief?
choices: Plainridge has higher elevation; Deepvalley has higher relief
Deepvalley has higher elevation and higher relief
Deepvalley has higher elevation; Plainridge has higher relief
Plainridge has higher elevation and higher relief
hints: Answer the elevation question first by comparing the heights above sea level: 80 meters versus 1,800 meters.
Answer the relief question second by checking each description separately: one place has sharp changes, the other has little change.

problemText: Three places are described below. Use the elevation and relief of each to sort them correctly. Mesa View sits 2,200 meters above sea level with ground that stays nearly level. Craggy Peak sits 2,100 meters above sea level with ground that rises and falls sharply nearby. Flatshore sits 5 meters above sea level with ground that stays nearly level. Which statement correctly places all three places by their elevation, and separately by their relief?
choices: By elevation from highest to lowest: Craggy Peak, Mesa View, Flatshore. By relief from high to low: Craggy Peak, Flatshore, Mesa View.
By elevation from highest to lowest: Mesa View, Craggy Peak, Flatshore. By relief from high to low: Craggy Peak, Mesa View, Flatshore.
By elevation from highest to lowest: Craggy Peak, Flatshore, Mesa View. By relief from high to low: Mesa View, Craggy Peak, Flatshore.
By elevation from highest to lowest: Flatshore, Craggy Peak, Mesa View. By relief from high to low: Mesa View, Flatshore, Craggy Peak.
hints: Start with elevation alone: line up the three heights above sea level (2,200, 2,100, and 5 meters) from highest to lowest. Then ignore elevation completely and check only the relief descriptions.
Remember that a place can sit higher than another but still have less relief — you must check both facts separately for each place.

problemText: A landform has a flat surface across a wide area and rises far above the land next to it. What is this landform called?
choices: A plain
A plateau
A valley
A hill
hints: Think about the two questions: does it stand HIGH or LOW, and is its top FLAT or does it narrow to a point?
This one is high AND flat on top, just like a plateau is described.

problemText: Picture a piece of land that rises only slightly above the ground around it and has smooth, rounded slopes instead of steep, jagged sides. The top does not form a sharp point. Which landform does this describe?
choices: A mountain
A plateau
A hill
A plain
hints: Does this rise HIGH and steep, or not as high with gentler slopes?
Mountains come to narrow peaks; this one has rounded slopes, so it must be the lower, gentler landform.

problemText: A student sees a strip of lowland sandwiched between two mountain ranges on either side. What defines this strip as a valley?
choices: It is low ground that has mountains nearby but not always directly on both sides of it
It is surrounded by mountains with steep peaks that rise above it on all edges
It has a completely flat and level surface with water running through the middle
It is low ground that sits between higher land on both sides
hints: A valley's definition depends on what sits NEXT to it, not just how low it is.
Remember: a valley is squeezed between higher land on two sides, which is what makes it a valley and not just any low ground.

problemText: Two regions both stand well above the land surrounding them. Region X has a flat top that stretches for many miles, with edges that drop steeply. Region Y narrows to a single sharp peak and climbs more steeply than Region X. Which region is which landform, and why must you check both height AND shape to tell them apart?
choices: Region X is a plateau and Region Y is a mountain; you must check both because two landforms can stand high but have different top shapes
Region X is a hill and Region Y is a mountain; you must check both because height determines the name while shape determines the slope angle
Region X is a mountain and Region Y is a plateau; you must check both because steepness of climb is what tells them apart from all other landforms
Region X is a plateau and Region Y is a hill; you must check both because the number of peaks on top is what separates high landforms from each other
hints: Both regions stand high, so HEIGHT alone won't tell them apart. What is different about their TOPS?
A flat top makes a plateau; a narrow peak makes a mountain. You need both the height question AND the shape question to name them correctly.

problemText: A student says: 'A plain is the same thing as a valley because both are flat and level.' Explain why this statement is wrong by describing what makes a valley different from a plain in terms of what lies next to it.
choices: A valley is surrounded by higher land on both sides that defines its shape, whereas a plain is simply a wide flat area and requires no specific features bordering it
A valley has higher land on both sides that borders it, while a plain is a wide stretch with no requirement for what sits next to it
A plain is defined by being surrounded by valleys on multiple sides, whereas a valley is only recognized when it appears between exactly two hills of equal height
A valley must contain running water to be called a valley, but a plain can be either wet or dry depending on the season and climate region
hints: Both can be flat, so flatness is not what makes them different. What is the key property of what borders a valley?
A valley is DEFINED by the higher land on both its sides. A plain is just a wide, level stretch and is NOT defined by what surrounds it.

problemText: An imaginary continent has four different landforms. Landform A stands very high with steep sides and comes to a narrow rocky peak. Landform B is high and flat on top with steep drop-offs at its edges. Landform C rises gently above its surroundings with rounded slopes and moderate height. Landform D stretches for hundreds of miles with almost no change in elevation, and nothing around it stands much higher. One student claims that A, B, and C are all the same because they all stand above their surroundings, while D is different because it does not. Explain why this claim misses an important property that actually makes three of these landforms different from each other, even though they all stand high.
choices: The claim is wrong because A is a mountain with a peak, B is a plateau with a flat top, C is a hill with rounded slopes, and D is a plain with no high points, so comparing only height ignores the shape property that defines each
The claim is wrong because the shape of the TOP or SURFACE is the second property that must be checked; A has a point, B has a flat top, C has rounded slopes, so they are three different landforms

The claim is wrong because A, B, and C all require checking a second property beyond height—whether the top is pointed, flat, or rounded—whereas D is determined by height alone since it has no surface variation
The claim is wrong because A stands very high with steep sides while B and C stand at moderate heights, making them different categories even though all three are above their surroundings
hints: The student checked only one question: does it stand high? What is the SECOND question from the lesson that must also be answered?
Remember the two-question routine: high or low compared to surroundings, AND is the top flat or does it come to a point? Check how A, B, and C are different in their second property.
